title: What triggers a Full GC (Old Gen full, Metaspace full, System.gc(), promotion failure), and why is it dangerous in production (stop-the-world, pause scales with heap)?

s1_definition.profdef: A Full garbage collection is a collection that processes the entire heap, both the Young and Old generations, and usually Metaspace as well, rather than just the Young generation. Common triggers are the Old generation filling up, Metaspace filling up, an explicit `System.gc()` call, and promotion failure, which occurs when the Old generation cannot accept objects being promoted from the Young generation. Full GC is dangerous in production because it is typically a stop-the-world event that pauses every application thread, and because its pause time scales with the size of the live set in the whole heap, so large heaps can produce pauses of seconds, violating latency requirements.
s1_definition.analogy: A Minor GC is like a quick tidy of the busy front counter at National Bank of India while the branch keeps serving customers. A Full GC is like the manager deciding to lock the front doors, stop all tellers, and do a complete top-to-bottom inventory of the entire building including the deep archives. Nothing gets served while it happens, and the bigger the building and the more folders inside, the longer everyone waits outside. It happens when the archives are full, when the blueprint room is full, when head office orders a full audit, or when the front counter has survivors but the archive has no room to accept them.
s1_definition.oneliner: A Full GC collects the whole heap and is triggered by a full Old generation, full Metaspace, an explicit System.gc, or promotion failure, and it is dangerous because it stops every thread for a pause that grows with the heap size.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Full garbage collection is a collection that processes the entire heap, both the Young and Old generations, and usually Metaspace as well, rather than just the Young generation. Common triggers are the Old generation filling up, Metaspace filling up, an explicit `System.gc()` call, and promotion failure, which occurs when the Old generation cannot accept objects being promoted from the Young generation. Full GC is dangerous in production because it is typically a stop-the-world event that pauses every application thread, and because its pause time scales with the size of the live set in the whole heap, so large heaps can produce pauses of seconds, violating latency requirements.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A Minor GC is like a quick tidy of the busy front counter at National Bank of India while the branch keeps serving customers. A Full GC is like the manager deciding to lock the front doors, stop all tellers, and do a complete top-to-bottom inventory of the entire building including the deep archives. Nothing gets served while it happens, and the bigger the building and the more folders inside, the longer everyone waits outside. It happens when the archives are full, when the blueprint room is full, when head office orders a full audit, or when the front counter has survivors but the archive has no room to accept them.

**One line to remember:** A Full GC collects the whole heap and is triggered by a full Old generation, full Metaspace, an explicit System.gc, or promotion failure, and it is dangerous because it stops every thread for a pause that grows with the heap size.

sections.s2_technical:
A Full GC differs from a Minor GC in scope. A Minor GC touches only the Young generation and is frequent and cheap. A Full GC processes the whole heap, both generations, and typically also cleans Metaspace, which makes it far more expensive. In the older collectors it is a single stop-the-world phase; in region-based collectors like G1 a true Full GC is a fallback that is supposed to be rare. Understanding what triggers it is the key to avoiding it.

The first trigger is the Old generation filling up. Objects promoted from the Young generation accumulate in the Old generation, and when it cannot fit more, the collector must reclaim dead objects there, which requires a collection of the old space and therefore a Full GC in the classic collectors. The second trigger is Metaspace filling up: if class metadata exhausts the Metaspace limit, the JVM runs a Full GC to try to unload unused classes before failing. The third trigger is an explicit call to `System.gc()`, which is a hint that, when honored, typically forces a full collection; this is why calling System.gc in production is discouraged, because it manually inflicts the most expensive collection. A small banking example of the danger is `System.gc();` placed inside a transfer path, which turns every transfer into a potential multi-hundred-millisecond pause.

The fourth trigger is promotion failure, sometimes called a concurrent mode failure in certain collectors. During a Minor GC, surviving young objects need to be promoted into the Old generation, but if the Old generation does not have enough contiguous space to accept them, the promotion fails and the JVM falls back to a Full GC, often with compaction, to make room. This is especially likely when the Old generation is fragmented or nearly full, or when allocation rate spikes. Large objects that are allocated directly into the Old generation, bypassing the Young generation, can also hasten this.

The danger in production has two parts. First, a Full GC is almost always stop-the-world, meaning it pauses every application thread, so during the pause no transfers are processed, no requests are answered, and health checks can even time out and cause an orchestrator to kill the instance. Second, the pause time scales with the amount of live data in the whole heap, because the collector must trace and often compact all reachable objects; a small heap might pause tens of milliseconds, but a large multi-gigabyte heap with lots of live data can pause for seconds. In a latency-sensitive banking service with strict service-level objectives, a multi-second global pause is a serious incident. The senior guidance is to prevent Full GCs rather than tune them: size the heap and generations correctly, avoid unbounded caches and memory leaks that fill the Old generation, never call System.gc in application code, and choose a modern low-pause collector like G1, ZGC, or Shenandoah for large heaps, since ZGC and Shenandoah keep pauses in the low single-digit milliseconds even on very large heaps by doing most work concurrently.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's reporting service holds an unbounded in-memory cache that slowly fills the Old generation. Eventually the Old generation is full, a Full GC fires, and every request pauses for over a second, breaching the latency objective. This is exactly the Old-generation-full trigger and its stop-the-world danger.

Problem 2 — A well-meaning developer added System.gc in a scheduled job, forcing periodic Full GCs that pause the whole service on a timer. This is exactly the explicit-System.gc trigger, which should never be in production code.

In the mini-project we build a cache that can be bounded or unbounded, read the Full-GC collector bean to count full collections and total pause time, and demonstrate that an unbounded cache plus a System.gc call drives up Full GC count and pause time, while a bounded cache keeps it near zero. The demo logs the difference.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the demo
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/fullgc/FullGcDemo.java

# Run with GC logging; a small heap makes Full GC pressure visible
java -Xms128m -Xmx128m -Xlog:gc* \
     -cp out com.bank.fullgc.FullGcDemo

# Compare with an UNBOUNDED cache (edit maxSize huge) to see Full GCs climb,
# or disable the explicit call entirely with:
java -XX:+DisableExplicitGC -Xms128m -Xmx128m -cp out com.bank.fullgc.FullGcDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a bounded report cache limited to ten thousand entries, half a million one-kilobyte report blobs inserted, then an explicit System.gc call.

Step 1: At startup the reporter reads the old-generation collector bean and logs a baseline Full GC count and pause time, usually zero.

Step 2: The loop inserts five hundred thousand blobs, but the cache is bounded, so once it reaches ten thousand entries it evicts the oldest on each new insert. The evicted blobs become garbage and are reclaimed by cheap Minor GCs in the Young generation, so the Old generation does not fill with surviving blobs.

Step 3: The report after the bounded cache shows the Full GC count still low, because the bound prevented the Old generation from filling. This demonstrates that controlling what lives long prevents the Old-generation-full trigger.

Step 4: The explicit System.gc call is made. This is a hint that the JVM honors by running a Full GC, which stops all threads, traces the whole heap, and cleans Metaspace. The report afterward shows the Full GC count incremented and the total pause time risen.

Step 5: The logs make the cause and effect clear: a bounded cache keeps Full GCs near zero, while System.gc manually forces one, which is exactly the kind of avoidable pause that hurts a latency-sensitive banking service.

```text
[INFO] [startup] Full GCs = 0, total Full GC pause = 0 ms
[INFO] bounded cache holds 10000 entries (evicting)
[INFO] [after bounded cache] Full GCs = 0, total Full GC pause = 0 ms
[WARNING] calling System.gc() — forces a Full GC (do NOT do this in prod)
[INFO] [after explicit System.gc()] Full GCs = 1, total Full GC pause = 18 ms
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Full garbage collection is a collection that processes the entire heap, both the Young and the Old generations, and usually Metaspace too, rather than just the cheap Young generation. That full scope is what makes it expensive, so understanding its triggers is how I avoid it. There are four classic triggers I always name. The first is the Old generation filling up, because objects promoted from the Young generation accumulate there, and when it can no longer fit more, the collector must reclaim the old space, which is a Full GC in the classic collectors. The second is Metaspace filling up, where the JVM runs a Full GC to try to unload unused classes before it fails. The third is an explicit call to System dot gc, which is a hint that, when honored, typically forces a full collection, and that is precisely why calling it in production is discouraged. The fourth is promotion failure, which happens during a Minor GC when the surviving young objects need to be promoted but the Old generation has no room, so the JVM falls back to a Full GC, often with compaction, to make space.

The reason a Full GC is dangerous in production comes down to two properties. First, it is almost always stop-the-world, meaning it pauses every single application thread, so while it runs no transfers are processed, no requests are answered, and health checks can even time out and cause an orchestrator to kill the instance. Second, its pause time scales with the amount of live data in the whole heap, because the collector has to trace and frequently compact all the reachable objects. A small heap might pause for tens of milliseconds, but a large multi-gigabyte heap with a lot of live data can pause for whole seconds. In a latency-sensitive banking service with strict service-level objectives, a multi-second global pause is a genuine incident.

In my experience the two most common self-inflicted causes are an unbounded in-memory cache that slowly fills the Old generation until a Full GC fires, and a well-meaning but harmful System dot gc call that forces full collections on a timer. I fixed the first by bounding the cache with an eviction policy so the evicted entries die cheaply in the Young generation and the Old generation stays healthy, and I fixed the second simply by removing the call and, as a safety net, running with explicit GC disabled.

The senior guidance I close on is that you prevent Full GCs by design rather than tune them after the fact. I right-size the heap and generations, I eliminate unbounded caches and memory leaks that fill the Old generation, I never call System dot gc in application code, and for large heaps I choose a modern low-pause collector like G1, ZGC, or Shenandoah, because ZGC and Shenandoah do almost all of their work concurrently and keep pauses in the low single-digit milliseconds even on very large heaps. Then I monitor Full GC count and pause time in Prometheus and alert the moment one occurs, because in a healthy service a Full GC should be a rare and investigated event, not a routine one.

---

keyPoints: Old Generation full or cannot accommodate promoted objects
Metaspace full — too many classes loaded
CMS/G1 concurrent mode failure — concurrent GC cannot keep up
Full GC is dangerous in production: stops ALL threads (stop-the-world)
